    <meta name="DC.Description" xml:lang="en" content="Lipschitz decomposition is a useful tool in the design of efficient algorithms involving metric spaces. While many bounds are known for different families of finite metrics, the optimal parameters for n-point subsets of 𝓁_p, for p > 2, remained open, see e.g. [Naor, SODA 2017]. We make significant progress on this question and establish the bound β = O(log^{1-1/p} n). Building on prior work, we demonstrate applications of this result to two problems, high-dimensional geometric spanners and distance labeling schemes. In addition, we sharpen a related decomposition bound for 1 < p < 2, due to Filtser and Neiman [Algorithmica 2022]." >

<div class="ltx_abstract" id="abstract">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
<p class="ltx_p">Lipschitz decomposition is a useful tool in the design of efficient algorithms
involving metric spaces.
While many bounds are known for different families of finite metrics,
the optimal parameters for <math id="m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point subsets of <math id="m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>, for <math id="m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p>2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>,
remained open, see e.g. [Naor, SODA 2017].
We make significant progress on this question
and establish the bound <math id="m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=O(\log^{1-1/p}n)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>log</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>.
Building on prior work, we demonstrate applications of this result to two problems,
high-dimensional geometric spanners and distance labeling schemes.
In addition, we sharpen a related decomposition bound for <math id="m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1<p<2" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo><</mo><mi>p</mi><mo><</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>,
due to Filtser and Neiman [Algorithmica 2022].</p>
</div>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">The pursuit of approximating metric spaces by simpler structures has inspired
the development of fundamental concepts,
such as graph spanners <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite>
and low-distortion embeddings into various spaces <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>,
both of which have a wide range of algorithmic applications.
Many of these results, including for instance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>,
rely on various notions of decomposition of a metric space into low-diameter clusters,
and these decompositions are most often randomized.
One extensively studied notion,
see e.g. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>,
is <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Lipschitz decomposition</em> (also called <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">separating decomposition</em>),
which informally is a random partition of a metric space into low-diameter clusters,
with a guarantee that nearby points are likely to belong to the same cluster.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 1.1</span></span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Lipschitz decomposition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>)<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span>
</h6>
<div id="S1.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,\rho)" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> be a metric space.
A distribution <math id="S1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></math> over partitions of <math id="S1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math> is called <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_upright"><math id="S1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\beta,\Delta)" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>-Lipschitz</em> if</span></p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">for every partition </span><math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P\in\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D})" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>supp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">, all clusters </span><math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C\in P" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">
satisfy </span><math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{diam}(C)\leq\Delta" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>diam</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">; and</span></p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">for all </span><math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x,y\in X" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">,</span></p>
<table id="S1.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_left"><math id="S1.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pr_{P\in\mathcal{D}}[P(x)\neq P(y)]\leq\beta\cdot\tfrac{\rho(x,y)}{\Delta}," display="block"><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>Pr</mi><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≠</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mstyle displaystyle="false"><mfrac><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padright"></td>
</tr></tbody>
</table>
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where </span><math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(z)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> denotes the cluster of </span><math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline"><mi>P</mi></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> containing </span><math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z\in X" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">
and </span><math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{diam}(C):=\sup_{x,y\in C}\rho(x,y)" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>diam</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.111em" rspace="0.167em">sup</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.</span></p>
</div>
</li>
</ol>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Typical applications require such decompositions
where <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></math> is not known in advance,
or even multiple values of <math id="S1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></math> (say for every power of <math id="S1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline"><mn>2</mn></math>).
We naturally seek small <math id="S1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline"><mi>β</mi></math> and thus define
the (optimal) <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">decomposition parameter of <math id="S1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,\rho)" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math></em> as</p>
<table id="S1.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_left"><math id="S1.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}(X):=\inf_{\beta\geq 1}\Big{\{}\beta:\ \text{$\forall\Delta>0$, every%
 finite $X^{\prime}\subseteq X$
admits a $(\beta,\Delta)$-Lipschitz decomposition}\Big{\}}," display="block"><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><munder><mo lspace="0.111em" movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">inf</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munder><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">{</mo><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.778em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mtext>, every finite </mtext><mrow><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>⊆</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mtext> admits a </mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mtext>-Lipschitz decomposition</mtext></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padright"></td>
</tr></tbody>
</table>
<p class="ltx_p">and we extend this to a family of metric spaces <math id="S1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi></math>,
by defining <math id="S1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}(\mathcal{X}):=\sup_{X\in\mathcal{X}}\beta^{*}(X)" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.111em" rspace="0.167em">sup</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Obtaining bounds on the decomposition parameter of various metrics
(and families of metrics) is of significant algorithmic importance,
and we list in <a href="#S1.T1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> several known bounds.
One fundamental example where we know of (nearly) tight bounds
is the metric space <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}^{d}" display="inline"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup></math>, for <math id="S1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\geq 1" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>,
which stands for <math id="S1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline"><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></math> equipped with the <math id="S1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> norm.
For <math id="S1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in[1,2]" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, we have <math id="S1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}(\ell_{p}^{d})=\Theta(d^{1/p})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
due to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>,
and for <math id="S1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in[2,\infty]" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> we have <math id="S1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}(\ell_{p}^{d})=\tilde{\Theta}(d^{1/2})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
due to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>
(see discussion therein about an incorrect claim made in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>).<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>Throughout, the notation <math id="footnote1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{O}(f)" display="inline"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>O</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> hides <math id="footnote1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{poly}(\log f)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>poly</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> factors,
and <math id="footnote1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O_{\alpha}(\cdot)" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>α</mi></msub><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> hides a factor that depends only on <math id="footnote1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math>.</span></span></span>
Observe that an upper bound for <math id="S1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X=\ell_{p}^{d}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> immediately extends to all subsets of it,
implying in particular a bound for the family <math id="S1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi></math> of all finite subsets of <math id="S1.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}^{d}" display="inline"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup></math>.
These bounds depend on <math id="S1.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>, and are thus most suitable for low-dimensional settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We focus on finite metrics <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math>, aiming to bound <math id="S1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}(X)" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> in terms of <math id="S1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=|X|" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></math>,
which is often useful in high-dimensional settings.
For instance, it is well-known that <math id="S1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}=\Theta(\log{n})" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
the family of all <math id="S1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point metric spaces <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>.
To write this assertion more formally,
define <math id="S1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}_{n}(X):=\beta^{*}(\{X^{\prime}\subseteq X:\ |X|=n\})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>⊆</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.778em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
and then the above asserts that <math id="S1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}_{n}(\ell_{\infty})=\Theta(\log n)" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>,
where we used that every finite metric embeds isometrically in <math id="S1.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{\infty}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub></math>.
For the family of <math id="S1.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point <math id="S1.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> metrics,
combining <math id="S1.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}(\ell_{2}^{d})=\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{d})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mi>d</mi></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
with the famous JL Lemma <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite> immediately yields <math id="S1.p4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}_{n}(\ell_{2})=O(\sqrt{\log n})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>,
which is tight by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>.
For <math id="S1.p4.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point <math id="S1.p4.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> metrics, <math id="S1.p4.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1<p<2" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo><</mo><mi>p</mi><mo><</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>,
we have <math id="S1.p4.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}_{n}(\ell_{p})=\frac{O(\log^{1/p}{n})}{p-1}" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>log</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> due to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>,
nearly matching the lower bound of <math id="S1.p4.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}_{n}(\ell_{p})=\Omega(\log^{1/p}{n})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>log</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math> from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>.
However, for <math id="S1.p4.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point <math id="S1.p4.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> metrics, <math id="S1.p4.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p>2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, to the best of our knowledge,
the only known upper bound is <math id="S1.p4.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}_{n}(\ell_{p})=O(\log n)" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>,
obtained by trivially applying the results for general <math id="S1.p4.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point metric spaces.
The following question was raised by Naor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, Question 1]</cite>,
see also <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>, Question 83]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_question">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Question 1.2</span></span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>)<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span>
</h6>
<div id="S1.Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Is it true that for every <math id="S1.Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in(2,\infty)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, <math id="S1.Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}_{n}(\ell_{p})=o(\log{n})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>? More ambitiously, is it true that <math id="S1.Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}_{n}(\ell_{p})=O_{p}(\sqrt{\log{n}})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>?</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Our main result, in <a href="#S1.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 1.3. ‣ 1.1 Our Results ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.3</span></a>,
answers the first part of this question in the affirmative.
Additionally, we show in <a href="#S2" title="2 Decompositions and Spanners in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑>𝟐 ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>
an analogous result for another notion of decomposability
that was introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> (and we call capped decomposition)
and is particularly suited for high-dimensional geometric spanners.</p>
</div>

<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Geometric Spanners.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">A <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">spanner with stretch <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\geq 1" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math></em> (in short a <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic"><math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>-spanner</em>)
for a finite metric <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=(X,\rho)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a graph <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G=(X,E)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>,
that satisfies <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(x,y)\leq\rho_{G}(x,y)\leq t\cdot\rho(x,y)" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>G</mi></msub><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
for all <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x,y\in X" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>,
meaning that the shortest-path distance <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{G}" display="inline"><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>G</mi></msub></math> in the graph <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>
approximates the original distance <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(x,y)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> within factor <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>,
where by definition every edge <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{u,v\}\in E" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> has weight <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(u,v)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
Of particular interest are spanners that are <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">sparse</em>,
meaning they contain a small number of edges, ideally linear in <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=|X|" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
Another important parameter is the <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">lightness</em> of a spanner,
defined as the total weight of its edges divided by the weight of a minimum spanning tree of <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math>.
Clearly, the lightness is at least <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline"><mn>1</mn></math>.
These spanners are called geometric because the input is a metric space
(rather than a graph).
They are natural and useful representations of a metric, and as such,
have been studied extensively, see the surveys <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>.
Spanners for <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point metrics in low-dimensional spaces
(e.g., in fixed-dimensional Euclidean space or doubling metrics)
are well-studied and well-understood.
For instance, metrics with doubling dimension <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{ddim}" display="inline"><mi>ddim</mi></math>
admit <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1+\varepsilon)" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>ε</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>-spanners
with near-optimal sparsity <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n(1/\varepsilon)^{O(\operatorname{ddim})}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>ε</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ddim</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
and lightness <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1/\varepsilon)^{O(\operatorname{ddim})}" display="inline"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>ε</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ddim</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">However, in high-dimensional spaces, our understanding of spanners is rather limited.
Har-Peled, Indyk, and Sidiropoulos <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> showed that
every <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point Euclidean metric admits,
an <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(t)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>-spanner with <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{O}(n^{1+1/t^{2}})" display="inline"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>O</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> edges for every <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\geq 1" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
Filtser and Neiman <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> extended this result to all metric spaces
that admit a certain decomposition that we call capped decomposition (<a href="#S2.Thmtheorem4" title="Definition 2.4. ‣ 2.2 Capped Decomposition in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑∈(𝟐,∞) ‣ 2 Decompositions and Spanners in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑>𝟐 ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Definition</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>),
showing that in those spaces, it is possible to construct spanners that are both sparse and light.
In particular, they showed that every <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point subset of <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>, <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1<p\leq 2" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo><</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>,
has an <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(t)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>-spanner with <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n^{1+\tilde{O}(1/t^{p})}" display="inline"><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>O</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msup></math> edges and lightness <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n^{\tilde{O}(1/t^{p})}" display="inline"><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>O</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></math> for every <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\geq 1" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
It remained open whether the spaces <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> for <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in(2,\infty)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
admit the aforementioned capped decomposition.
To the best of our knowledge, all known spanners for these spaces
have a tradeoff of stretch <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(t)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> with sparsity <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(n^{1+1/t})" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.1 </span>Our Results</h3>

<div id="S1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Our main contribution is the construction of a Lipschitz decomposition
for finite <math id="S1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> metrics, <math id="S1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\geq 2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.Thmtheorem3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 1.3</span></span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span>
</h6>
<div id="S1.Thmtheorem3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S1.Thmtheorem3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in[2,\infty]" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
Then <math id="S1.Thmtheorem3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}_{n}(\ell_{p})=O(\log^{1-1/p}{n})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>log</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>.
That is, for every <math id="S1.Thmtheorem3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point metric <math id="S1.Thmtheorem3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\subset\ell_{p}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>⊂</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> and <math id="S1.Thmtheorem3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta>0" display="inline"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, there exists an <math id="S1.Thmtheorem3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(O(\log^{1-1/p}{n}),\Delta)" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>log</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>-Lipschitz decomposition of <math id="S1.Thmtheorem3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Previously, this bound was known only for the extreme values <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=2,\infty" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow></math>,
and in these cases it is actually tight.
More precisely, for <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> our bound coincides with the well-known result
<math id="S1.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}_{n}(\ell_{2})=\Theta(\sqrt{\log{n}})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>,
and for <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=\Omega(\log{n})" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
it is known that <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}_{n}(\ell_{p})=\Theta(\log{n})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>,
because all <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point metrics embed into <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> with <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(1)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>-distortion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>.
For intermediate values, say fixed <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in(2,\infty)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>,
our bound is the first one to improve over <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(\log n)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>,
which applies to all <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point metrics,
and leaves a gap from the <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega(\sqrt{\log{n}})" display="inline"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> lower bound
that follows from Dvoretzky’s Theorem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We compare our bound with those for other metric spaces
in <a href="#S1.T1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">The proof of <a href="#S1.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 1.3. ‣ 1.1 Our Results ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.3</span></a>
appears in <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Lipschitz Decomposition in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑∈(𝟐,∞) ‣ 2 Decompositions and Spanners in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑>𝟐 ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>,
and has interesting technical features.
It relies on <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">two</em> known decompositions of finite metrics,
one for general metrics and one for Euclidean metrics,
that are composed via a metric-embedding tool called the Mazur map.
Our decomposition method is data-dependent, i.e., not oblivious to the data,
and we discuss this intriguing aspect
in <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Lipschitz Decomposition in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑∈(𝟐,∞) ‣ 2 Decompositions and Spanners in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑>𝟐 ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sections</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> and <a href="#S5" title="5 Future Directions ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx1" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Note added in proof.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Shortly after this work was posted online,
two groups working in parallel to each other <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>
improved our result in <a href="#S1.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 1.3. ‣ 1.1 Our Results ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.3</span></a>
to <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}_{n}(\ell_{p})=O_{p}(\sqrt{\log{n}})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math> for every <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2<p<\infty" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo><</mo><mi>p</mi><mo><</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></math>,
thereby resolving in the affirmative also
the second part of <a href="#S1.Thmtheorem2" title="Question 1.2 ([40]). ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref">˜<span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.2</span></a>.
These two papers design a recursive process that relies on
the technique developed here for proving <a href="#S1.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 1.3. ‣ 1.1 Our Results ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.3</span></a>,
see each paper for its dependence on <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx2" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Geometric Spanners for <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\geq 2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝒑</mi><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">≥</mo><mn>𝟐</mn></mrow></math>.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We then use similar ideas to obtain a new bound for another notion of decomposability,
that was introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> and we call capped decomposition;
and this immediately yields geometric spanners in <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>, for <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\geq 2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
While for <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> these spanners coincide with the known bounds from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>,
for fixed <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2<p<\infty" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo><</mo><mi>p</mi><mo><</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></math>, our spanners are the first improvement
over the trivial bounds that hold for all metric spaces.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.Thmtheorem4" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 1.4</span></span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span>
</h6>
<div id="S1.Thmtheorem4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S1.Thmtheorem4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in[2,\infty)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math id="S1.Thmtheorem4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\geq 1" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
Then every <math id="S1.Thmtheorem4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point metric <math id="S1.Thmtheorem4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\subset\ell_{p}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>⊂</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> admits an <math id="S1.Thmtheorem4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(t)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>-spanner of size <math id="S1.Thmtheorem4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{O}\left(n^{1+1/t^{q}}\right)" display="inline"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>O</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and lightness <math id="S1.Thmtheorem4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{O}\left(n^{1/t^{q}}\right)" display="inline"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>O</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>,
where <math id="S1.Thmtheorem4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q\in(1,2)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is such that <math id="S1.Thmtheorem4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=1" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>p</mi></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>q</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">The proof of this theorem appears in <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Capped Decomposition in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑∈(𝟐,∞) ‣ 2 Decompositions and Spanners in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑>𝟐 ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>,
and includes both the spanner construction, which follows <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>,
and our new bound for capped decomposition, which is the main technical result.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx3" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Geometric Spanners for <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\leq 2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝒑</mi><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">≤</mo><mn>𝟐</mn></mrow></math>.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We also sharpen the known spanner results for <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> spaces with <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1<p<2" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo><</mo><mi>p</mi><mo><</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>,
which say that every <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point subset admits an <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(t)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>-spanner
with <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n^{1+O(\log^{2}{t}/t^{p})}" display="inline"><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>log</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msup></math> edges and lightness <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n^{O(\log^{2}{t}/t^{p})}" display="inline"><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>log</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></math> for every <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\geq 1" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>.
We improve upon this result by eliminating the <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log^{2}{t}" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>log</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> factor in the exponent.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.Thmtheorem5" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 1.5</span></span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span>
</h6>
<div id="S1.Thmtheorem5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S1.Thmtheorem5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in(1,2]" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math id="S1.Thmtheorem5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\geq 1" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
Then every <math id="S1.Thmtheorem5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point metric <math id="S1.Thmtheorem5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\subset\ell_{p}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>⊂</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> admits
an <math id="S1.Thmtheorem5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(t)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>-spanner of size <math id="S1.Thmtheorem5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{O}(n^{1+1/t^{p}})" display="inline"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>O</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
and lightness <math id="S1.Thmtheorem5.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{O}(n^{1/t^{p}})" display="inline"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>O</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">The proof of this theorem, presented in <a href="#S3" title="3 Spanners in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑∈(𝟏,𝟐) ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, follows the construction of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>,
but replacing a key step, in which they rely on results from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>,
with results from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>.
Interestingly, our improved spanner bound “matches” the bounds of <a href="#S1.Thmtheorem4" title="Theorem 1.4. ‣ Geometric Spanners for 𝒑≥𝟐. ‣ 1.1 Our Results ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.4</span></a>,
up to duality between <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math> and <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx4" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Distance Labeling Schemes.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Distance labeling for a metric space <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,\rho)" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
assigns to each point <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in X" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> a label <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l(x)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>,
so that one can later recover (perhaps approximately)
the distance between any two points in <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math>
based only on their labels (without knowledge of the metric space).
It was formulated in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>,
motivated by applications in distributed computing,
and has been studied intensively, see e.g. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>.
An immediate corollary of our main result in <a href="#S1.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 1.3. ‣ 1.1 Our Results ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.3</span></a>
is a distance labeling scheme for finite metrics in <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> for <math id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p>2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>,
as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.Thmtheorem6" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 1.6</span></span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span>
</h6>
<div id="S1.Thmtheorem6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S1.Thmtheorem6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in(2,\infty)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
Then the family of <math id="S1.Thmtheorem6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point metrics in <math id="S1.Thmtheorem6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>
with pairwise distances in the range <math id="S1.Thmtheorem6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1,\Delta_{\text{max}}]" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">max</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math>
admits a distance labeling scheme with approximation <math id="S1.Thmtheorem6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(\log^{1/q}{n})" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>log</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
and label size <math id="S1.Thmtheorem6.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(\log{n}\log{\Delta_{\text{max}}})" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁢</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">max</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> bits,
where <math id="S1.Thmtheorem6.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q\in(1,2)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is such that <math id="S1.Thmtheorem6.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=1" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>p</mi></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>q</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">A formal definition of the distance labeling model
and a proof of <a href="#S1.Thmtheorem6" title="Theorem 1.6. ‣ Distance Labeling Schemes. ‣ 1.1 Our Results ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.6</span></a>
appear in <a href="#S4" title="4 Distance Labeling ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.2 </span>Related Work</h3>

<div id="S1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We focus on Lipschitz decomposition and on capped decomposition,
that was introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>,
but the literature studies several different decompositions of metric spaces
into low-diameter clusters, see e.g. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>.
In particular, the notion of padded decomposition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>
is closely related and was used extensively,
see for example <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>.
While a Lipschitz decomposition guarantees that nearby points are likely to be clustered together,
a padded decomposition guarantees that each point is, with good probability,
together with all its nearby points in the same cluster.
Remarkably, if a metric space admits a padded decomposition then it admits
also a Lipschitz decomposition with almost the same parameters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>,
however the other direction is not true, as demonstrated by <math id="S1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}^{d}" display="inline"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>d</mi></msubsup></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">The problem of computing efficiently the optimal decomposition parameters
for an input metric space <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,\rho)" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> was studied in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>.
Specifically for Lipschitz decomposition, they show that <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}(X)" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> can be <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(1)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>-approximated in polynomial time (in <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Decompositions and Spanners in <math id="S2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">ℓ</mi><mi>𝒑</mi></msub></math> for <math id="S2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p>2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝒑</mi><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">></mo><mn>𝟐</mn></mrow></math>
</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">In this section we consider finite subsets of <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> for <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in(2,\infty)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
We first present (in <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Lipschitz Decomposition in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑∈(𝟐,∞) ‣ 2 Decompositions and Spanners in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑>𝟐 ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>)
a new Lipschitz decomposition,
which proves <a href="#S1.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 1.3. ‣ 1.1 Our Results ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.3</span></a>.
Next, we show (in <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Capped Decomposition in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑∈(𝟐,∞) ‣ 2 Decompositions and Spanners in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑>𝟐 ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>)
a new construction of capped decomposition,
which is a related notion of decomposability
that was introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> without a concrete name.
Finally we obtain (in <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Spanners in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑∈(𝟐,∞) ‣ 2 Decompositions and Spanners in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑>𝟐 ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>) new spanners,
which prove <a href="#S1.Thmtheorem4" title="Theorem 1.4. ‣ Geometric Spanners for 𝒑≥𝟐. ‣ 1.1 Our Results ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.4</span></a>.
This is actually an immediate corollary of our capped decomposition,
by following the spanner construction of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Lipschitz Decomposition in <math id="S2.SS1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">ℓ</mi><mi>𝒑</mi></msub></math> for <math id="S2.SS1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in(2,\infty)" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝒑</mi><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">∈</mo><mrow><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟐</mn><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">,</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">∞</mi><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Before presenting the proof of <a href="#S1.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 1.3. ‣ 1.1 Our Results ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.3</span></a>,
we first provide the intuition behind the proof.
A common approach in many algorithms for metric spaces
is to embed the given metric into a simpler one (e.g., a tree metric),
solve the problem in the target metric,
and then pull back this solution to the original metric.
For our purpose,
of constructing a Lipschitz decomposition of <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\subset\ell_{p}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>⊂</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math>, <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p>2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>,
a natural idea is to seek a low-distortion embedding of <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math> into <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>,
because we already have decompositions for that space,
namely, <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}_{n}(\ell_{2})=O(\sqrt{\log{n}})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>.
Ideally, the embedding into <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> would be <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">oblivious</em>,
meaning that it embeds the entire <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> (not only <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math>) into <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>,
but unfortunately such an embedding does not exist
(it would imply oblivious dimension reduction in <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> for <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p>2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>,
which is provably impossible <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>).
We get around this limitation by employing a <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">data-dependent</em> approach,
where the decomposition depends on the input set <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math>.
More precisely, we use Mazur maps,
which provide a low-distortion embedding from <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math> to <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>,
but only for sets of bounded diameter (see <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem3" title="Corollary 2.3. ‣ 2.1 Lipschitz Decomposition in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑∈(𝟐,∞) ‣ 2 Decompositions and Spanners in ℓ_𝒑 for 𝒑>𝟐 ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Corollary</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>).
We thus first decompose <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math> into bounded-diameter subsets
by applying a standard Lipschitz decomposition
(that is applicable for every <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point metric).
The final decomposition is obtained by pulling back
the solution (clusters) we found in <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We proceed to introduce some technical results
needed for our proof of <a href="#S1.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 1.3. ‣ 1.1 Our Results ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Lipschitz Decompositions of Finite ℓ_𝑝 Metrics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.3</span></a>.
The first one is a well-known bound for Lipschitz decomposition of a finite metric.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 2.1</span></span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>)<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span>
</h6>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Every <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>-point metric <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,\rho)" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> admits an <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left(O\left(\log n\right),\Delta\right)" display="inline"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>-Lipschitz decomposition for every <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta>0" display="inline"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Next, we define the <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Mazur map</em>,
which is an explicit embedding <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{p,q}:\ell_{p}^{m}\to l_{q}^{m}" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>m</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msubsup><mi>l</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>m</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow></math> for <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1<q<p<\infty" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo><</mo><mi>q</mi><mo><</mo><mi>p</mi><mo><</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></math>.
The image of an input vector <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline"><mi>v</mi></math> is computed in each coordinate separately,
by raising the absolute value to power <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p/q" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> while keeping the original sign.
The next theorem appears in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>,
